title: Verifiable rewards: grading without a teacher
summary: What a reward is, what makes one verifiable, and how the two rewards behind R1-style training (format and correctness) work, including the design choices and blind spots hiding inside them.
learningObjectives: Explain what a reward is in reinforcement learning and what the model does and does not get to see.
Decide whether a task has a verifiable reward and describe how you would check it.
Explain why rule-based rewards were preferred over reward models for training reasoning.
Describe the format reward and the correctness reward and why correctness should be worth more.
Explain why a group of attempts that all score the same gives the model nothing to learn from.
Name what verifiable rewards cannot see, such as lucky guesses and readability.

interactive.title: Grade an answer yourself
interactive.caption: Edit the model's answer and watch the format and correctness rewards update live. Try deleting a tag, writing "18 or 26", or emptying the think block, and predict each score first.

studyGuide.mentalModel: Picture a teacher marking a huge pile of maths tests with only an answer key. They do not read the working; they check the boxed answer against the key and tick or cross. They also give a small mark for putting the answer in the box. The model is a student who never sees the key, only its marks, and slowly works out which habits earn ticks.
keyIdeas: A reward is a number saying how good an attempt was. The model only ever sees the score, never the right answer.
A reward is verifiable when a short, reliable program can decide it, for example comparing a final number or running test cases.
Rule-based rewards are cheap and hard to fool, which is why DeepSeek-R1 used them for maths and code instead of a reward model.
The format reward checks the think and answer tags; the correctness reward checks the final answer. Correctness should be worth more.
Learning needs contrast: if every attempt at a question scores the same, there is nothing to learn from it.
Verifiable rewards grade the outcome, so they reward lucky guesses and ignore readability.
misconceptions: "The model is shown the right answer during RL." It only receives a score for its own attempt.
"A verifiable reward checks that the reasoning is correct." It usually checks only the final answer and the format.
"Stricter rewards are always better." Too strict and a beginner model scores zero everywhere, which gives it nothing to learn from.
"The format reward is just cosmetic." It tells the grader where the answer is and gives the model an early, learnable signal.
recallPrompts: In one sentence, what is a reward function?
Give two tasks with verifiable rewards and two without.
Why might a reward model be a risky grader for reasoning?
Why should correctness be worth more than format?
Why does a group of eight attempts that all score 0 teach the model nothing?
Name one thing a verifiable reward cannot see.
studyGuide.explainBackPrompt: Explain to a friend how a computer can grade a maths word problem without a teacher, why that is so useful for training a reasoning model, and one way that kind of grading can miss the point.

quiz.prompt: During reinforcement learning with a correctness reward, what does the model receive for each attempt?
options: The full worked solution
Only a score for that attempt
The right answer and an explanation
A list of its mistakes
quiz.explanation: The model only gets a number. It never sees the gold answer. Over many attempts it learns to do more of whatever scored well.

quiz.prompt: Which task has the most clearly verifiable reward?
options: Writing a moving poem about the sea
Giving good career advice
Writing a function that must pass a set of unit tests
Summarizing a novel in an engaging way
quiz.explanation: Unit tests give a clear pass or fail that code can check. Poems, advice and engaging summaries depend on taste, so no short program can grade them reliably.

quiz.prompt: You give format a weight of 2.0 and correctness a weight of 1.0. What is the risk?
options: The model may learn that tidy but wrong answers are the fastest way to a high score.
Training will run out of GPU memory.
The model will stop using the think tags.
There is no risk; weights do not matter.
quiz.explanation: With format worth more than correctness, a tidy wrong answer (2.0) beats a messy right one (1.0). Keep correctness worth more so being right always wins.

quiz.prompt: A model makes 8 attempts at a hard question and every one scores 0. What does it learn from that question?
options: It learns to avoid all eight answers equally, which is very useful.
It learns the right answer from the zeros.
It learns to write shorter answers.
Nothing: no attempt scored better than another, so there is no contrast to learn from.
quiz.explanation: Learning comes from some attempts beating others. When every score is the same, there is no signal. That is why format rewards and a well-matched dataset matter early on.

quiz.prompt: A model writes nonsense working but its final number happens to be right. What does a correctness reward give it?
options: Zero, because the working is wrong
Half marks
Full marks, because only the final answer is checked
A penalty for guessing
quiz.explanation: Verifiable rewards grade the outcome, not the reasoning. Over many questions lucky guesses mostly wash out, but it is a real blind spot.

exercises.title: Design a verifier for three tasks
hints: Ask: is there one right answer, and can a short program compare against it?
Decide what to be lenient about (decoration) and what to be strict about (substance).
For a task that is not verifiable, say which part of it could still be checked.
